en: Explanatory Remarks:
The present text has been edited to facilitate word searches. It is based on the manuscript of the transliteration of the *Abhisamācārikā-Dharma* of the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādins.
Grammatical errors and the like have been left uncorrected; however, preferred readings are occasionally provided for conspicuous scribal errors.
The symbols and editorial features are as follows:
(1) Letters enclosed in parentheses indicate that they should be supplied.
(2) Letters that appear to be erroneously written are underlined; immediately following such letters, a suggested correction is provided within parentheses.

(3) Letters in blue and underlined are to be omitted; no suggestion is provided following them. This rule also applies to the omission of the *virāma*. (4) Letters enclosed within [square brackets] indicate that they are obscure.
(5) An illegible character (*akṣara*).
(6) Symbols that appear to indicate *virāma* are replaced by a comma (“,”).
(7) Symbols that appear to be *siddham*,
Etcetera are replaced by “*”.
(8) Deletions in the manuscript are not indicated.
(9) J. refers to the Jinananda edition.
(10) Compounds in which a hiatus occurs are hyphenated.
*Abhisamācārikadharma*
Ch.499a22 Homage to the Buddha.
The beginning of the *Abhisamācārika* [rules]:
The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī, the teacher of gods and humans; having established the introduction in detail, it was now the *poṣadha* of the Saṅgha, and the Venerable Nandana...
The Elder Upananda and the second Elder asked the donors and patrons:
"Noble ones, what did the entire Saṅgha of bhikṣus say to us, O long-lived ones? Who is not coming now?"
The monks said, "The elder of the Saṃgha is not coming. They then said, "Look here, friends! Let us first abandon our work and come; we shall pay homage at the feet of the entire Saṃgha."
And we shall establish this object of religious merit;
however, the elder of the Saṅgha does not come.
Now, having returned later and recited the four *pārājika* rules in brief, he did not assign the merit of the offering.
He did not give a formal discourse;
having risen, he departed. [This was said by] the junior monks.
They asked: "Venerable ones, has the Elder of the Saṃgha not arrived? The monks said: "He has arrived and he has departed. Those junior monks also said: "The Elder of the Saṃgha... [J.2]
"The coming of the hero is known, but not his going.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "Summon Nandana. He was then summoned. The Blessed One said, "Is it true, Nandana, that this is indeed called the Saṃgha’s Poṣadha?"
The Blessed One related all of that in detail: "The junior monks are complaining: 'There is neither going nor coming.'"
"It is known," he said.
"Yes, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, the senior monk of the Saṃgha should conduct himself in this manner during the Poṣadha ceremony.
What, then, is the manner in which the senior monk of the Saṃgha should conduct himself during the Poṣadha?"
On whichever day the Saṃgha’s Poṣadha occurs,
on that day the Elder of the Saṃgha must take note.
"What is today's *poṣadha* for the Saṅgha? Will it be on the fourteenth, the fifteenth, or a transitional *poṣadha*? What meal should come first?"
What is the time for the post-meal [meditation]? At how many *pauruṣa* shadows of the sun will it take place?
Where will it be?
Either in a hall for abandonment, or in a hall for attendance,
or in a fire-hall,
or in a circular pavilion.
In whatever region and on whatever day the *poṣadha* of the Saṃgha occurs,
the senior monk of the Saṃgha [should recite] the five *sūtras* in detail.
These should be studied:
as many as there are four Pārājika rules and the verses concerning the non-existent.
If, regarding the rule for frequent hearing, the Saṃgha has not yet arrived, [then...]
The senior of the Saṅgha should announce it wherever it will take place:
"Venerable sirs, today is the Poṣadha of the Saṅgha, whether on the fourteenth or the fifteenth day, or the Poṣadha for the transition [of the season]."
It will take place at such-and-such a place,
either in the hall for exertion or in the hall of attendance.
"In the assembly hall, whether before the meal or after the meal,
let the venerable ones pass by; it was not even announced by me."
Where one must sit with a small stool,
one should indeed go to the place for the Poṣadha ceremony beforehand and have it sprinkled with water.
The ground should be thoroughly swept and a coating of cow dung should be applied. An arrangement of seats should be prepared.
If resources are available, the counting sticks should be washed with scented water and strewn with flowers.
The senior of the Saṅgha must determine who will distribute the voting sticks, who will receive them,
and who will recite the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
Who will designate the sacrificial fee? Who will deliver the formal discourse? He who... (2a1)
He is a fool;
he should be requested [as follows]: "This person shall distribute the voting sticks for you; you shall receive the voting stick."
You recite the Prātimokṣa-sūtra, you speak it, you provide the exposition,
and you prescribe the dedication of merit. Therefore...
The voting stick should be distributed according to the request;
the second person should receive it. Furthermore, it is not permitted for the one distributing the voting stick to distribute it with unwashed hands.
Nor is it permissible for one who is wearing a hooded cloak or who is wearing sandals to cast the voting stick.
While distributing [the voting sticks],
one should first wash the hands, remove the head-covering,
take off the sandals, and, having arranged the robe over one shoulder, distribute the voting sticks.
Now, even when taking a voting stick (*śalākā*),
it is not permissible to do so while wearing a head-covering or while standing in sandals.
To take the voting stick (*śalākā*):
one must first arrange one’s robe over one shoulder, rub the hands together, remove the head-covering (*oguṇṭhikā*), and take off the sandals; at that time, the voting stick should be taken.
(2a3) The voting sticks have been distributed, the monks have been counted, and the assembly has been announced; the donor and patron must be questioned.
"Will you stay, or will you go?
If they say, "We are going," then [the donor] should offer the gift of merit.
They should be established;
they should be made to rejoice in the gift of Dharma; and they should be instructed with a discourse on the Dharma.
They should be encouraged, they should be inspired,
and they should be gladdened.
(2a4) They should be exhorted.
Now, if they say, "We shall stay," one should say:
"First go outside for a moment; wait there."
The community of monks will perform the *poṣadha* ceremony at such a time that the donor and master of the gift...
They have run out.
Therefore, the reciter of the sūtra should know:
if [the time] does not yet pass...
It becomes cool;
it is neither too hot, nor are the monasteries situated too far away,
nor are the monks weak from old age, nor are they afflicted by illness.
Or they become weak in intelligence;
or else, the monks do not remain seated in comfort due to fear of lions, fear of tigers, or fear of thieves.
If they wish to hear the Prātimokṣa Sūtra in detail,
the Prātimokṣa Sūtra should be recited in detail. But now, if it is too cold...
Or it may become excessively hot;
or the monks may be weakened by old age or weakened by illness;
or there may be fear of lions, fear of tigers, or fear of thieves for the monks.
(2a6) And they do not wish to hear the Prātimokṣasūtra in detail; having recited the four Pārājika rules in brief, the remainder is for those who have heard it frequently.
Then, after the verse, one should do as is appropriate;
if it is now the entire night,
then one should make a formal request.
"You shall speak."
As requested, while speaking throughout the entire night, having spent it with a rain of Dharma,
the donor and master of generosity should be instructed with a discourse on the Dharma.
They should be exhorted, encouraged, gladdened, and inspired;
they should be allowed to act according to their ease.
May the Venerable Ones rejoice! Thus...
The senior monk of the Saṃgha must perform the Poṣadha ceremony; if he does not perform it, it constitutes a transgression of the rules of proper conduct.
He transgresses the dharmas.
The Blessed One was dwelling in Śrāvastī, the teacher of gods and humans.
Having related the introductory narrative in detail, it was now the *poṣadha* day of the Saṃgha.
The Venerable Nandana was the elder of the Saṃgha, and Upanandana was the second elder. The elder of the Saṃgha had arrived, and the monks had arrived, but the second elder did not come.
Now the donors and masters of the gift, having taken up the articles of merit,
will wait upon the complete assembly of the Bhikṣu-saṃgha and pay their respects to it.
And we shall establish this object of religious merit.
Then they asked: "Venerable sir, the entire community of monks has said, 'Long-lived one, this is not so; who indeed has not come?'"
They said, "The second Elder is not coming.
Then they complained,
"We have come here having abandoned our very work, yet we go to pay homage at the feet of the entire Saṃgha."
We shall pay homage and we shall establish the gift of merit.
The second elder also did not come;
having waited for just a moment and remained there,
they dedicated their gift of merit and departed.
Now, having arrived at such an unseasonably late hour, the elder of the Saṅgha complained:
"The Blessed One is inflicting disciplinary punishment upon us."
[The monk] Mottika;
the monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Summon Upananda. He was then summoned, and the Blessed One said:
"It is true, Upananda; now it is the Saṃgha’s Poṣadha. Then the Blessed One related all of that in detail, up until—
The elder of the Saṃgha also complained: "The Blessed One is inflicting punishment upon us. The second elder, Monttika, said:
"Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, the second elder should proceed in this manner during the *poṣadha* ceremony."
Now, how should the second elder proceed regarding the *poṣadha*?
On whatever day the *poṣadha* of the Saṃgha occurs, [he should act as follows].
If the elder of the Saṃgha is not capable,
the second elder must ascertain:
"Is today the Uposatha of the Saṃgha on the fourteenth day?"
Whether it be the fifteenth-day [uposatha], or the junction-uposatha, will it be a night-uposatha or a day-uposatha? Will it be before the meal?
"After the meal,
where will it take place?
In the assembly hall, or in the meditation hall, or in the circular pavilion?"
Whether it be at a place for cutting [grass] or at a sitting hall— wherever one happens to be— one should announce there:
"Venerable sirs, today is the Poṣadha of the Saṅgha, whether on the fourteenth or the fifteenth day."
Now, if the senior of the Saṃgha is not capable,
the second senior must have the place for the Poṣadha sprinkled with water as a matter of course.
It should be thoroughly swept;
a coating of cow dung should be applied; the preparation of a seat should be made; and if one has the means, the voting sticks should be washed with scented water.
If the senior of the Saṃgha who is to be honored with flowers is not capable [of performing the task],
the second senior must determine who will distribute the voting sticks (*śalākā*) and who [will assist].
He shall distribute the voting sticks.
Who will recite the Prātimokṣa-sūtra? Who will speak it?
Who will prescribe the sacrificial fee?
Who will deliver the formal discourse? Who is capable?
He will be there;
he is to be requested:
"You shall distribute the voting sticks."
"You shall receive [the portion] as long as you cause the formal discourse to be performed.
Therefore, while distributing the voting sticks (*śalākā*), it is not permissible [to act otherwise].
Or, having covered one's head with a cloth, or being mounted on sandals, or with hands unwashed,
to distribute the voting sticks; rather, having washed one's hands and [removed] the sandals...
Having removed [the upper robe] and arranged it over one shoulder, the voting stick (*śalākā*) should be distributed. Furthermore, by one receiving the voting stick,
it is not permissible to receive the stick while wearing a hood, or while wearing sandals, or with hands that have not been washed.
Then, having removed their hand-ornaments and having taken off their sandals, they should receive the voting sticks with one shoulder bared.
When the voting sticks have been distributed, the monks have been counted,
and the assembly has been announced,
then the donors and patrons should be asked: "What?"
"You shall dwell here, or you shall go, if they speak thus:
'We are going;
therefore, a gift of merit (deyadharma) should be established, and the gift of merit should be made the object of rejoicing.'"
A formal discourse should be delivered; having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dharma, they should be dismissed.
Now, if they say, "We shall stay," [then they may remain].
It should be said: "The Saṃgha shall wait outside for a moment; the Saṃgha will perform the Poṣadha ceremony. When the donors and patrons have departed, then [the ceremony shall proceed]."
The reciter of the Sūtra should know:
if it is either too cold or too hot,
or if the monks are weak due to old age.
Either they become weak due to illness, or the monastic cells are situated very far apart, or there is fear of lions, fear of tigers, or fear of thieves;
or perhaps the monks do not [practice] in detail.
They become desirous of hearing;
[therefore] the four *pārājika* rules should be recited in brief.
The remainder consists of the *Abhīkṣṇaśruti* and the verses;
thereafter, one should act as is convenient.
Now, when it is neither too cold nor too hot, and the cells are not situated too far away,
and the monks are seated comfortably and desire to hear the teaching in detail—
Then the Prātimokṣa-sūtra should be recited in detail;
thereafter, one may act as one pleases.
Now, if it is the entire night [of the observance],
and the senior of the Saṃgha is not capable, he should be requested by the second senior.
"You must speak, you must speak! Speak as requested; let us spend this entire night with a rain of Dharma for the sake of the donors and patrons."
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse, they should be dismissed;
thereafter, one may act as one pleases.
May the venerable ones take delight; may the venerable ones take delight. One must accomplish this through heedfulness. Thus [said] the second Elder. (3a6)
On the day of the Poṣadha, one must undertake [the observances];
if one does not undertake them, one transgresses the rules of proper conduct.
The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī, the teacher of gods and humans.

Having related the introductory narrative in detail, it was now the *poṣadha* day of the Saṃgha. The Venerable Nandana was the elder of the Saṃgha, and Upanandana was the second elder. Although they had arrived, the monks did not come to the assembly hall. The donors and patrons asked, "Noble ones, is the community of monks complete? [The elders replied: "The monks..."
He said, "Long-lived one, why is it that these do not come?
The monks replied,

Then they complained: "We have come here repeatedly, abandoning our various works of labor,
for the sake of the Saṃgha as a whole."
"We shall pay homage at his feet and we shall establish our religious gifts (deyadharma). Yet these noble ones do not come even to the Osaratiya."
The elder of the Saṃgha and the second elder were indignant,
saying, "The Blessed One inflicts disciplinary punishment upon us, yet upon these [others]..."
The monks Montika and Etaka reported this matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "Summon those monks. They were then summoned.
The Blessed One said: "It is true, monks; now this is indeed the Uposatha of the Saṅgha.
The Blessed One [repeated] all of that.
He reports it in detail,
until the elder of the Saṃgha and the second elder both become indignant.
“The Blessed One is giving us a disciplinary punishment.
Those little boys said, “Yes, Blessed One.”
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, everyone must conduct themselves in this manner during the *poṣadha*. What [is it]?"

Thus, now, everyone should conduct themselves in this manner on the *poṣadha* day; everyone must know [this]: "Is today the first day of the fortnight, the second, or up to the fifteenth? If, now, anyone...

He asked: "Venerable sir, what should not be said now? And furthermore, how indeed was it written? [The reply was: "It must necessarily have been written with split bamboo splinters or with reed splinters using thread."
Having announced it, it should be tied up either at the gate-chamber, or in a palace, or in a hut for allowable things;
having dug in stakes, [it should be tied] at the door.
It should be established. Now, whoever is a "month-walker" or a "fortnight-walker," he must circulate [the bowl] one by one.
Regarding the daily procedure as it has been instructed, everyone must know this: "Now, this is the *poṣadha* of the Saṃgha;
the elder of the Saṃgha is not capable [of conducting it]."
The second elder is not capable;
he who is capable there must take cognizance of it.
Is today the Saṃgha’s Poṣadha— whether on the fourteenth day, or the fifteenth day, or a transitional Poṣadha, or a Poṣadha by day or by night?
Whether before the meal or after the meal, at how many fathoms' length of shadow will it be? Will it be in the hall for exertion, or in the hall of attendance, or in the circular pavilion?
Whether at a secluded walking path or a secluded sitting area,

by his very nature,
go to the place for the *poṣadha* ceremony and sprinkle the place for the *poṣadha* ceremony.

who shall distribute the voting sticks? Who shall receive the voting sticks?

Now, if he is not capable,

You distributed the voting sticks;
you received them; you recited the Prātimokṣa; you spoke; you assigned the offerings; you caused the formal discourse to be delivered.

nor while having one's head covered.

"What will you do? Will you stay or will you go?"— if they say this:
"Let us go," [he said],

Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dharma, they should be dismissed.
Now, however, they say: "We shall dwell [here]."
It should be said:
"First, you outsiders, please wait for a moment; the Saṅgha will perform the Poṣadha ceremony. At that time...

it should be understood by means of a summary of the sūtra.
If it is neither too cold nor too hot, and there is no fear of thieves, nor fear of lions, nor fear of tigers,
and [the place] is not very far away;
Or there may be monasteries where the monks are neither weakened by old age nor weakened by illness;
they are comfortably seated and desire to hear in detail. Then, the Prātimokṣa-sūtra should be recited in detail.
Now, if it is already late at night,
the reciters should be requested [to speak].
"You must speak; you must speak."
As requested, having spoken,
and having spent the entire night with a rain of Dharma,
one should instruct, inspire, and encourage the donors and patrons with a discourse on the Dharma, until...

May the venerable ones rejoice!

In this manner, all should conduct themselves during the Poṣadha; if they do not so conduct themselves, they incur an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.

The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī as the teacher of gods and humans. Having set forth the introductory narrative in detail, it so happened that the Saṅgha now had a meal provided by outsiders; the Venerable...
The Elder Nandana, the second Elder Upanandana, and the monks have arrived;
yet the Elder of the Saṅgha does not come,
and the rice has grown cold.
The soup becomes cold;
the ghee solidifies, the meat solidifies, and the side dishes become cold.
Then the donors and masters of the gift ask:
"Noble one, did the entire community of monks say this?
Long-lived one, who indeed has not come?
They replied, "The elder of the community has not come."
Then they complained:
"We have abandoned our very livelihoods..."
"Come, let us go; we shall serve the entire community of monks.
But the elder of the Saṅgha did not come. Then, having arrived later, he—
Having eaten briefly and assigned the ritual fee (*dakṣiṇā*), he does not give a detailed discourse,
nor does he instruct the donor or benefactor with a discourse on the Dharma.
He encourages, inspires, and gladdens [them].
Having risen and departed, the junior monks asked, "Has the Elder of the Saṅgha arrived? They replied, "He has arrived and he has departed. Then...
The monks reflected that neither the coming nor the going of the senior elder of the Saṅgha was discernible. They reported this matter to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, being addressed, said: "Is it true, Nandana, that there is indeed food for the Saṅgha outside [the monastery]? "It is so, [Nandana]," he replied.
The Elder Upananda said, "The second Elder," and the Blessed One related all of that in detail,
until the junior monks expressed their reproach.
As long as neither the coming nor the going of the senior of the Saṅgha is perceived,
he said:
“Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
“In that case, the elder of the Saṅgha should conduct himself in this manner at the head of the meal.”
Now, how should the senior of the community (saṃghasthavira) conduct himself at the head of the meal? The senior of the community must be aware of this.
Whose alms-food today is it?
Is it all for the community from both sides, or for the entire community, or for a specific cell, or individual alms-food in the village or at the monastery? This is now [the case].
If someone invites the Saṃgha for a meal on the following day,
the Elder of the Saṃgha must not now give his consent by merely going back and forth.
Then, indeed, the senior of the Saṅgha must ascertain who is inviting him:
is it a newcomer or a traveler, a householder or one who has gone forth, a woman or a man?
The boy or girl should be asked:
"What is your name?
What is your clan? What..."

The attendant should ask those parents, "In what country do you live? What is your house like? On which street is it? Which way does the front of the house face? Having asked for the description of the house along with its location, he should then settle there.
Nor should one now think, "I have already consented," and thus remain clinging to that place.
Rather, one who is naturally inclined to travel for a month or a fortnight should be sent forth, saying, "Go!"
"Find out what is being prepared.
"In that case, there may be many births for me, or I may be dead, or my joints severed, or consumed by fire, or some calamity from the royal court, or perhaps a *ḍhossā*."
If rakes or sons of the wind, with the intention of causing harassment, should invite him, he should go and ask:
"Is there any lay follower here named so-and-so? If they should say: [Yes].
"We have no such lay follower by that name who could say,
'The community of monks has been invited by him; what is prepared or cooked?'"
If they say, "One must know whose food it is, for whom it is prepared,
and by whom it is cooked," [then] the community of monks has been deceived.
(1.52) Having arrived, if there is a favor to be rendered, that favor should be accomplished; if it is not a favor [to be rendered], there are alms-foods [to be given];
the alms-foods should be designated; the alms-foods...
If there is no clamor, one should strike the ghaṇṭī and say:
"Venerable sirs, the community of monks has been deceived; each of you should seek your own livelihood. By all [of them].
One should enter for alms in regular succession.
Now, if they say to you,
"Venerable sir, this..."

When it is announced, "The community of monks has entered and is established," then, having struck the *gaṇḍī* with a resonant sound, if it is winter, [the meal] should be taken at the appropriate time.
One should enter [the dwelling], lest the time should pass. Now, if it is the summer season, because of the cold [of the night],...
One should enter at the appropriate time.
Now, when the time for the rainy season retreat has arrived, one should enter [the monastery] as soon as possible, lest the proper time should pass by due to obstacles caused by the gods.
If, however,
it does not become clear, and a long time has passed, and he wishes to go somewhere for someone's sake—
The monk should be told:
"When you are about to visit such-and-such a family, if it should be prepared, do not decline."
Now, he must not think, "I have been summoned by him," and thus be struck down by the deeds of Bhadrapāla;
rather, indeed, [he should respond].
One should approach as if on a mission;
having entered, one should ascertain how the seats have been arranged.
If,
on an occasion requiring an auspicious rite, a seat that is too far to the right or not to the left has been prepared, one should sit down in exactly that manner.
Now, if a place has been designated for the funeral rites of the deceased,
one should sit down exactly as instructed; furthermore, it is not permissible for those entering to bring in goods.
They were going along jumping over bronze vessels, jumping over boys and girls,
and jumping over merchandise; indeed, they were avoiding the bronze vessels.
They should enter while keeping boys and girls at a distance; furthermore, it is not permissible for them to sit down immediately upon arriving and departing.
Rather, they should [take] a seat with their hand.
It should be examined whether there might be various forms of fetuses present there,
or whether bronze vessels might have been set out.
Then, indeed, by touching with the hand,
one should know [the state] of those who are prone to sloth.
Or it should be caused to be given to those who are ill;
or if that person is now one who has not practiced giving.
If he becomes stingy, one must not then remain indifferent;
rather, it should be said: "O long-lived one, you must certainly give alms-food to them."
Now, if the donors and patrons say, "Take them in order," and it is winter time, [the following] should be said:
"No, no," [said the Blessed One].
"In many ways, the Blessed One has declared that the sick are limited; how can we possibly make the monastery empty? Time passes quickly."
"Give it to us.
Now, if it is the time of summer, or the rainy season, or night, and the time passes by for a long duration;
It should be taken in successive order;
then it must be understood by the senior of the Saṃgha from whom [the gift] is being given and likewise to whom.
An invitation must be extended; food is being given, and a great portion has been received. The senior of the Saṃgha (saṃghasthavira) should say: "For all [of you]..."

One should remain [there].

In that place,

there is no offense;
however, it is not permissible [to do so] at that time.
While chewing a tooth-stick,

using the left hand.

It is permissible to throw rice there;
one must know [the reason]:
whether many villagers have gone to another village, or whether robbers have fallen upon them, and so forth.
"They are not coming.
(II.p.9) Having had the monastery cleared by a single monk, [he] dismissed [them].
One should remain restrained.
Why do those living at the edge of the village not come? No.
Thus it is said: if they indeed come, rice must be placed for them as well; but if they do not come now, [then one should proceed otherwise].
At the proper time and place, having struck the gaṇḍī and paid homage to the cetiya, the village-dwelling monks should eat after the food has been served from the cooking pot into the bowls.
Having smeared them with clay, they should be set aside.
Now, if someone invites the forest-dwellers to a meal, it should be said:
"Invite the village-dwellers as well."
Then they said: "I have no faith there, nor do I have confidence; we must say that we will not accept [the invitation].
Now, if one invites even those from the outskirts of the village, food must be prepared.
The seats should be prepared;
the drinking water should be strained; and flowers should be arranged.
The incense should be prepared if the village-dwellers have not yet arrived,
even if the donor has already come.
He said,
"Venerable sir,
strike the gong; it is still early."
It still occurs today;
it should be said:
first of all, even today there are monks living in the vicinity of villages.
They do not come. Then he says:
"You [monks] living in the vicinity of the village, strike! (32a3)
"They will come. What should be done?
First, the gaṇḍī was sounded at length; [it proclaims] the dedication and the reliquary monument (caitya).
One should pay homage in detail. Having paid homage in detail, if the village-dwellers have arrived, one should eat.
Now, if the village-dwellers do not come,
one should prepare the seats.
They should sit down;
the server of the meal should say:
Who among the village-dwelling monks is the distributor of gains? If they say,
"I too, I too," it should be said [to them].
"Accept the alms-food for the monks living at the edge of the village. Now, if there is no one among them to receive the offerings,
the server [should place it] in one place for all of them.
Having brought back the alms-food, it should be placed in the Sangha’s storehouse for allowable items.
If they arrive at the proper time for eating, it should be given to them; but now, if...
They arrive at the wrong time, or they do not come at all;
it should be given to the novices or the monastery attendants, and it is no longer permissible [to give it to others].
Where the village-dwellers are attached to staying.
Furthermore, from time to time, one should vacate the forest dwelling; having washed one's feet and cleansed one's hands, one should pay extensive homage to the stupa.
If it is first of all the time for walking,
then by means of groves, at the roots of trees, on walking-paths, and in sitting postures— by means of standing, walking, and sitting— he [should practice].
Those devoted to yoga should pass their time either by engaging in the formal recitation of the teachings or by engaging in mental attention. Or else...

Now, when the time and place are right, having entered the monastery and exchanged greetings with the forest-dwelling monks, one should sit down on one's own respective seat. When the gaṇḍī has been struck, one should go after having paid homage to the stūpa and finished eating. Furthermore, not now...
Those living in the wilderness should be reviled and disparaged by those living near villages, saying,
"They are mere dwellers in empty houses."
By your wisdom,
you are like jackals dwelling in the forest all day long.
"You have been living together for years gathering alms.
Now indeed you must say: 'We have obtained forest lodgings that are difficult to dwell in, secluded, remote from inhabited areas, and places where one sleeps out of the way of people.'"
It is difficult to apply oneself to seclusion; it is hard to find delight in solitude, training the mind within for even a single night, let alone longer.
"Venerable one, you are doing well;
you are maintaining the forest dwelling as your bed and seat."
And this was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, as long as you dwell in forest lodgings,
only growth is to be expected."
There shall be no decline for you from wholesome qualities, nor shall Māra, the Evil One, find an opportunity regarding the True Dharma.
For the sake of disappearance and for the sake of delusion;
thus he cried out.
This is how one should proceed; this is how those living in the forest should practice.
If they do not practice in this way, [they are at fault].
He transgresses the rules of proper conduct.
The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī; at that time, on that occasion...
The venerable Nandana and Upanandana were in charge of the drinking water.
Now, those monks were rubbing their faces and hands right there by that very water.
They were washing their bowls and water-strainers; then, from early morning, Nandana and Upanandana washed the hands of the householders and strained the drinking water.
Having secured the water pavilion by closing its door and sealing it, the visiting monks entered their alms-round.
They arrived and searched for water, but they did not find any;
they then lamented, "What now?"
"This water pavilion has been protected, sealed, and established. When the monks heard this matter, they informed the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Call Nandana and Upanandana.
They were then summoned.
The Blessed One said: "It is true, monks, that Nanda and Upananda [did so]."
...pe... (as before) ...pe...
When a group of visiting monks arrived, they searched for drinking water.
They did not obtain it; they then complained, "Why has this water pavilion been made sealed and closed? They replied, "Yes."
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, in this regard, one should behave toward drinking water in this manner. Thus...
One should proceed with the washing of the feet.
Now, how should one proceed regarding water?
In this manner, one should proceed regarding the washing of the feet.
It is not permissible to pour water after it has been strained, and then to splash it about in the water pavilion.
If one has sealed [the door] and wishes to go elsewhere,
then indeed a water-carrier must first be assigned.
At the end of the new [robes],
either in order of seniority or according to who receives them first—
one or two [monks].
Whether there be three or as many as can manage it,
they should rise early and wash their hands.

Having filtered the water, one should prepare a vessel— whether it be a globular jar (*golaka*), a water-pot (*maṇika*), a camel-skin bag (*uṣṭrikā*), a small pitcher (*thaganaka*), a brass vessel (*ārañjara*), a bowl (*ghaṭṭa*), or a water-jar (*karaki*)— provided with a lid (*appihāṇa*). [This applies to] stone (*śilā*).
It should be bound by me with clay, or with wood, or with clear pieces of cloth.
It should be well-polished and placed so that the water remains clean;
it must not be used with a chicken-rope.
Having tied it, it should be set aside.
Pāṭala pills, or campaka pills, or sugar should be placed in those vessels; everything should be prepared in this manner.
So that they may become fragrant; therefore, if there is one water for drinking and another for washing the feet, the latter must be strained.
The water-pot should be filled with pure, filtered water.
The ritual water-jar should be filled;
the foot-washing basin should be filled.
The water-jar for the body should be filled;
and the monks' water-jars for hand-washing, for bowl-rinsing, and for general use, as well as their water-pitchers, should be filled.
It becomes as follows: just as the Śoṇa water at Pāṭaliputra [is] there at Rājagṛha.
In Vārāṇasī there is a lotus pond named Buddhavicīrṇā;
in Campā, the water of the Gaṅgā; and in Śrāvastī, [the water of the Pe...]
In Śāketa there is water supported by the earth;
in Mathurā, the Yamunā is not able to withstand that water.
To fill a permissible water-pot, an impermissible water-pot, or a chamber-pot;
or to give water for the hands, water for the feet, or drinking water;
or indeed, from that [source], for the purpose of drinking.
It should be given. Now, if the monk is faithful,
then if he fills his own auspicious water-pot from that very [source], there is no offense.

A monk’s eyes were paining him, and the physician said, "Venerable sir, wash your eyes with water from the *gotra*. Now, he may take a bowlful [of such water], and he may perform washing, dyeing, or cleaning with it.
He has need of water;
he asks the water-drawer, "I wish for water to be given. But she does not give it.
It is permissible to give water for one who is established in the lineage (*gotrastha*).
Then, indeed, the water for ritual purification (*pāridhovanīya*) should be given.
When about to drink water in the presence of a devotee, one should wash one's hands thoroughly,
wash the vessel thoroughly, and [use] pure water.
One should cause [the water] to be drawn;
by one taking the drinking water, it should be held with one hand.
It becomes free from worldly attachment.
Now, if it has suddenly become possessed of worldly attachment, one should wash it and [then...]
If the vessel or the cup becomes stuck to the lips,
one should rinse it and then drink;
now, one must not [lick] too much of the lip.
It should be cast [into the fire];
or the hair, or the forehead,
or indeed the lips [should be cast].
Having wiped it with the tips [of the fingers], it should be drunk;
from that very [portion], a small amount should be left over.
It should be discarded while washing with that same [residue] at the end.
While pouring out water,
one should observe whether anyone [is present] who might cause too much [water] to splash onto the lips or the hair.
Regarding the "ālaya": it should be removed from the forehead; having set that vessel aside in a secluded spot, one should place grass or a *kulika* leaf on top as a sign of recognition.
"If it is known to be unfit,
it should be washed again;
afterwards, while distributing the food and water, [one should wash] the hands."
Having made it well-polished.
...pe... (as before) ...pe...
One should hold the water with one hand,
while receiving the water-pot with the other, using either the inner fold of the robe or the outer fold.
Or it should be taken with an intermediate vessel,
using that very same interval.
It should be discarded. While moving about in the sauna, one should [place] the lips [of the mouth] near the water-carrier's bowl.
It should be bound [to the mouth].
While drinking, one should rinse the lips with the leaf-stalk and drink using the tips of the lips.
...pe... (as above) ...pe...
That very same thing must be done by one practicing for abandonment:
if there is a ground-covering, the vessels should be placed upon leaves and branches.
It should be placed on cow dung, or sand, or in vessels. If they are seated at the eighth or fourth part [of the assembly], one person should [speak] with a moderate voice.
One should recite while standing on the steps;
another should lead [the way]. Now, if they have sat down for meditation at very great distances from one another in succession, by one person...
It should be carried out.
...pe... (as before) ...pe...
Now it is permitted to wash one's face from the water used for rinsing, or to wash one's hands,
or to wash the bowl-strainer; but not now [is it permitted otherwise].
It is permissible to discard [the water] with a splashing sound;
it should be poured out by the mother. Now, it is no longer permissible to bathe from the rinsing-water vessel.
Whether it be to wash a robe or to boil dye;
now, when the monks are performing work on robes.
The water becomes turbid and the vessel is overflowing; now,
it may be taken by one who possesses evil views.
He said, "Venerable sir, give it;
I will bring more and give it to you. And so he gave it.
There is no offense. Having now taken that [water] and brought it, it should be given from time to time.
Now, if the monastery is without nearby water, [this applies].
Moreover, he drinks from that very same [vessel], performs his ritual rinsing from that very same one,
washes his hands from that very same one, or prepares the dye from that very same one.
There is no offense [if one acts thus]. This is how one should behave regarding water;
if one does not so act, one transgresses the rules of proper conduct (*ābhisamācārika-dharma*).
The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī. Now, those venerable ones...
The group of six, including Nandana and Upanandana, washed their feet in the grove at the foot of the tree;
having washed their feet, they poured out all the water.
Having placed the foot-washing stand upside down and having put on wet sandals, he did not even...
They avoided the mud but did not avoid the dust; while treading upon the mud, they continued to tread upon the dust as they walked a long distance.
Then monks arrived for the purpose of washing their feet. They...
Then they said:
"Venerable sirs, you should wash your feet with moderation; indeed, even regarding water, there must be moderation."
The Blessed One had likewise said that they [should not use] any external requisites for life; then those monks saw that the foot-washing basin was empty.
Now they complained,
"Why has this foot-washing basin been turned upside down?
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Summon Nandana, Upanandana, and the group of six."
They were then summoned,
and the Blessed One said:
"Is it true, monks?"
O Nandana, Upanandana, and you members of the group of six,
you go to the foot-washing trough and wash your feet with splashing sounds,
then discard the water and turn the foot-washing trough upside down.
"Having placed your wet feet in your sandals, do not avoid the dust nor the mud;
trampling through the mud and trampling through the dust, walk a long distance,
for monks are coming."
Having washed their feet at the foot-washing place, you said, "Venerable ones, wash your feet. Now, water was indeed permitted by the Blessed One.
The mother spoke thus. In the same way, when those monks saw that all their requisites for living had been turned upside down and placed in the foot-washing area,
they said, "Yes, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"It is a transgression for you, Nanda, Upananda, and the group of six;
therefore, foot-washing should be performed in this manner."
Thus, having washed one's feet, one should conduct oneself in this manner: now, how are the feet to be washed? Now, in what manner?
"One should proceed with washed feet.
The Blessed One then addressed the monks:
"Monks, you should wash your feet in this manner."
For example, Śāriputra the Elder:
monks, on one occasion the Elder Śāriputra was staying at Vaiśālī in the Mahāvana, in the Gabled Hall; then, at the very time for the morning meal, the Elder dressed himself.
Taking his bowl and robe, he entered the city of Vaiśālī for alms, with graceful and dignified deportment in his advancing and retreating, in his looking ahead and looking aside,
in his drawing in and stretching out [his limbs], and in his manner of wearing the outer cloak, the bowl, and the robes; he was inwardly composed.

With his senses withdrawn, with a mind established and having attained the state of natural reality, mindful and clearly comprehending, he walked for alms through the city of Vaiśālī like one who has performed his duty upon the Path.
Then the Elder was seen by another brahmin, and it occurred to that brahmin: "These..."
Thus, the sons of Kitikā—
those "little ascetics"— practice their deportment at the edge of the village and,
having run out, they cause disturbances.
Now, with a malicious mind, he followed closely behind the Elder, thinking, "I will wait right where this young ascetic breaks his deportment."
Right there on his head, I shall place a razor. Now, the Elder—
Endowed with a deportment equal to that of a village or a forest, having walked for alms in Vaiśālī, he emerged and returned to the monastery, O Elder.
Now, having placed the bowl in this dwelling, washed his hands, shaken out his outer robe (saṃghāṭī), and brought it inside,
he folded it double and placed it on the robe-rack; then, having filled the water-vessel with water.
Having spread out a seat and having placed a footstool nearby, he offered him sandals.
Having removed his sandals and approached, he washed his feet;
then the Elder poured water with his right hand.
He washed his feet with his left hand.
Then the elder washed his left leg, and [the other] washed his right leg.
The left foot has been washed; the right foot has been washed; the sandals and the parasol have also been washed.
Taking a sandal and making it into a pouch, he wiped the fastening of one sandal with it,
and he wiped the fastening of the second sandal with it.
The sole of one sandal was wiped, and the sole of the second sandal was wiped;
having set down the sandals, [he took] water from the water-jar with his left hand.
Having turned [the water] away, having washed the sandals and the foot-wiping cloth with the right hand,
having wrung them out, one should dry them in the sun; having poured out the water from the leather strap, one should wash one's hands.
Having washed the water-jar, having discarded the remaining water, and having dried it in the sun,
that brahmin,
seeing his conduct and sphere of activity, was then pleased.
With a serene mind, he said:
"Just as this water-pot has been used by you, Śāriputra, even that brass vessel for hot water belonging to the brahmins is not as pure as this."
"Indeed, water can be obtained from here to drink.
Then, the Elder revealed the Four Noble Truths to that brahmin whose mind was filled with faith: the Noble Truth of Suffering, and so forth.
The noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering,
and the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
Then, while remaining in that very place, that brahmin realized the fruit of stream-entry. Thereupon,
the monks said to the Blessed One:
"How is it that the Blessed One is pleased with this brahmin elder’s conduct and sphere of activity? The Blessed One said:
"It is not only now; at another time as well."
He is indeed satisfied with his conduct and sphere of activity. At another time, Blessed One;
at yet another time, monks—formerly, in the past—at this very place, there was a city named Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśi.

Now, there was a man of the foremost family, wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments; one who had abundant wealth, grain, treasuries, and granaries; one who possessed abundant gold, silver, assets, and utensils; and one who had many elephants, horses, goats, cattle, and sheep.
He was a laborer among his employees;
now he had a son who had been born not long ago. (34b2)
Then he was reared and raised by his mother and father;
when he was seven or eight years old, he would rise before his parents and go to rest after them, speaking kindly and never saying anything displeasing.
Then, the sons of good family who were his disciples and servants began to frequent the house of that merchant;
and his house was well-guarded.
And although they were well-guarded, they could not find an opportunity [to harm him].
Now, on one occasion, that merchant went to another gathering of his kinsmen, having been invited there.
Having stationed that boy as a night-watchman, he closed the door and remained guarding it while waiting. Then,
when the merchant had departed with his retinue, the boy closed the door of the house.
While he was guarding it, those sons of good family found an opportunity;
they then leaped over the wall and entered that house, and having lit torches and lamps, [they proceeded].
They searched; they saw that single boy and then asked him: "Boy, where [are you]?"
"Is it silver or gold for you?
He then replied,
"I do not know either."
"Search this empty house again and again; whatever you find there, take it.

Then, having searched again and again, they found a great heap of abundant gold and bullion made into a mound in the middle room of the house. He who was their chief of the band of thieves—[he was there].
He sat in the central hall of the house;
he was the commander-in-chief of the army.
Being thirsty, he said to that boy:
"O boy, I am thirsty; I wish to drink water. Then that boy, being of clean conduct, took a vessel.
Having washed his hands thoroughly and having rinsed the vessel well, he filled it with water.
Where the lamps were burning, he approached them; then,
having carefully observed [the situation], he approached the commander of the thieves' army,
saying, "Commander, drink!"
Then that bandit leader also observed everything as the boy was giving him water;
he then asked, "Ho, boy! For whose sake are you here?"
Having approached the base of the lamp, he then said:
"General, examine the drinking water;
let there be no grass or living creature in this water, lest it cause discomfort to the general."
[May it] be so. Now, that general was pleased by his conduct and sphere of activity;
[he thought: "O General, wait, wait! Let this man not [fall into the hands] of our executioners for the time being."

Even toward adversaries and enemies, he is desirous of their welfare and desirous of their benefit; how much more so toward his own mother, father, or kinsmen—how could he not possess a mind of loving-kindness toward them?
"If we [were to take] this gold and bullion from this boy who is so devoted to the Dharma..."
"We might be robbed by highwaymen, we might be captured,
or we might be executed by the royal court. Now, at that time—
The bandit general, having drunk water, summoned all those bandits and asked, "Who says this? Who am I to you? They then replied:
The general said,
"Sirs, I am satisfied with this boy’s conduct and sphere of activity in such and such a manner; if we [give] this gold to this most righteous one..."
"We might steal gold, or we might be robbed by other thieves; we might be captured, or even executed at the royal court—if it is agreeable to you. (35a2)
"Let us release him;
we shall steal the gold and silver of another. They then said, "As it pleases the commander."
Then he said to the boy:
"Come now, my boy, I give all this gold and bullion to you; the thieves have now been driven away."
When that boy had bolted all the doors, a deity spoke this verse:
"Those endowed with the virtues of proper conduct..."
But those men who train in proper conduct and do not train in improper conduct obtain abundant wealth, just like the giver of water.
Though seized by the core [of his sin], he was released because of his virtuous conduct.
Those who train in proper conduct and discipline become those who are not to be slain; endowed with the virtues of right conduct, they attain sovereignty over various stations.
Those who are worthy of execution become unworthy of execution by training in proper conduct (*ācāra*) and discipline (*vinaya*).
Therefore, a person should always be endowed with the quality of proper conduct.
Fierce bandits with blood-stained hands find satisfaction in such [people].
By means of conduct, those who were ignoble became noble and entered upon the state of being born as such.
On this matter, the Blessed One spoke these verses of Dharma:
"One should not strike a brahmin, nor should one release [a weapon] at him.
Fie on the slayer of a brahmin, and fie also on him who releases [the weapon] against him!"
The Blessed One said:
"It might occur to you, monks, that at that time and on that occasion, he was the son of a prominent family; it should not be viewed in this way."

This elder Śāriputra was that other commander of the thieves; this brahmin was [the one who followed him] even then, being pleased by his conduct and sphere of activity, and now too he is pleased by the elder’s conduct and sphere of activity.
Now, whenever this monk has gone out from the village...
Then, having shaken out the robe for entering the village and having thoroughly finished its preparation, it should be set aside.

and [prepare] a water-vessel and a broom.
Having removed the cloth lining, washed it, and wrung it out, the sandals should be cleaned.

It should be placed after wringing out the cloth so that no living beings are born [in it] or so that it does not become moldy.

and [wipe] the sole of one sandal.
It should be wiped.

They become exhausted;
therefore, he should be made to enter. Now then, (35b2)

one should indeed snap the fingers.

When they have washed their feet, then, at that moment, [the pillar].

The right foot is to be washed;

If there [is no water] there...

It should be placed inside that sandal;
nor is it permissible to sit at the foot-washing stand with one's head covered or with one's hands tucked under the armpits.
Furthermore, one should sit with one shoulder bared;
nor, moreover, is it now permissible [to sit] at the foot-washing place.

Whether engaged in the formal recitation (*uddeśa*), or engaged in mental attention (*manasikāra*), or having fallen into drowsiness while contemplating the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), he was unable to remain [seated]. Then, having washed his feet, he rose up.
One should go; one should go while avoiding the dust. Furthermore, it is no longer permissible to walk a long distance on foot with washed feet.
Now, when a monk is engaged in recitation,
if he walks while his feet are still wet, they must be washed again. Now then...
When it is the winter season, a monk sees who else will wash [the robe],
even if only with a piece of rag.
Or, having wiped [the feet] with the left hand, one should enter; in this manner the feet should be washed;
and in this manner one should conduct oneself after having washed the feet.
He does not practice;
he transgresses the rules of proper conduct.
The Blessed One was staying at Rājagṛha. Having set forth the introduction in detail, Jīvaka...
The physician for children requested of the Blessed One:
"May the Blessed One grant permission."
"It will be comfortable for the disciples who have disorders of wind, bile, and phlegm in the steam-heated bathhouse.
The Blessed One said:
Therefore, I authorize it;
this itself is the origin of the matter.
The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī. Now, the Saṅgha had a steam-bath house, and those venerable ones of the group of six [were there].
Having prepared [the bathhouse] as if for a ritual, having lit the fire, and having bolted the door, they sat there perspiring.
When the monks arrived, they knocked at the door. (36a3)
"Venerable ones, give us passage!
They then said,
"Let them come."
"Venerable ones,
the sauna has not yet become warm by the time the monks have assembled."
Having used up all the oil, having used up all the powder, having discarded all the water,
and having cast all the wood into the fire, he entered the steam bath.
They ran out and said,
"Venerable sirs, please enter; the sauna is heated."
Now, when the monks were touched by the sensation of cold,

the monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
Therefore, it should be addressed in this way:
"How is it now that [you act] thus?"
It must not be scratched. It is not permissible for a monk, while seated in the place of exertion (*prahāṇa*),
with the intention of causing agitation, to scratch his limb with a pebble or a rough piece of wood.
...to scratch. Now, however, when a monk is seated in meditation and is being bitten, he may [scratch] comfortably with the hollow of his thumb or the palm of his hand.
It must be removed.

Now, if it continues to be eaten again and again and becomes a source of disturbance for the practice of meditation (*prahāṇa*), one should depart after informing [the community]; nor is it permissible otherwise.
A monk [should not] sit together at the head of the meal or at the head of the refreshment.
Or, with the intention of causing agitation, one should scratch with a comb or a pebble, making a harsh "kharakaca-kharakaca" sound.
Now, if a monk is seated at the head of the meal or at the head of the refreshment, and some part of his body becomes itchy, [he should act as follows].
They are permitted to be used as hand-tools.
Furthermore, even if a monk scratches himself with a comb, a wooden stick, or a splinter, [it is permissible].
There is no offense. In that case, one should scratch it in such a way that the sound does not cause an interruption.
Now, if a monk is one who has an itch, he scratches it again and again.
The bowl of the one who sits immediately next to him should be given [to him].
[He should say: "Venerable sir, you have displaced my alms-food";
then he should depart.
It is not permissible, out of a desire for frivolity, to scratch one's limbs with a harsh scratching sound (*kharakaca-kharakaca*) in the presence of preceptors, teachers, or those who are senior.
Nor is it permissible, having loosened one's faculties, to scratch while speaking. Now, if some part of a monk’s body is itching, [he may scratch] with his thumb...
It should be rubbed with the hand or with the palm of the hand.
Now, if...
He strives to dispel it;
he digs again and again; having gone to one side, he should scratch [the itch].
In this way one should attend to scratching; if one does not so attend, [there is an offense].
He transgresses the rules of proper conduct.
The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī. Now, those venerable ones of the group of six—
Seated for the purpose of abandonment,
they yawn with an intention toward restlessness and stretch their limbs.
They rend with a *paṭa-paṭā* sound;
they roar with a *maḍa-maḍa* sound like lions or tigers; thus they gape.
They disturbed the yogācāra monks with noise.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
Therefore, it should be yawned in this way.
Now, how is it that one should yawn in this way?
It is not yet permissible for a monk who has sat down for meditation to,
with a mind intent on restlessness, lower his faculties and shake his limbs about with a clattering sound.
It should be broken [by a sound] just like that of a roaring lion or tiger. Now, if a yawn comes upon a monk who has sat down for meditation, he must not make his limbs sound "ṭaṭṭa-ṭaṭṭa."
Having opened the mouth by making a popping sound,
one should yawn.

One should divert [the mind] by [focusing on] the dark forehead, or one should massage it; or the nose should be massaged. Now, if one is unable to divert [the mind], then with full awareness, [one should focus on] the mouth.
Having closed [the mouth], one should yawn;
it should be done in such a way that the sound does not disturb the person immediately next to one. Now, if a monk continues to yawn again and again, [he should act accordingly].
One should either run out, stretch,
or depart after taking leave of those engaged in the practice of abandonment.
Furthermore, it is not permissible for one seated in the practice of abandonment to crack one's limbs with a grinding or creaking sound.
Now, if a monk’s limbs are in pain,
he should first extend one arm comfortably at a time when he has rested.
Having contracted that [first] leg,
the second leg should be extended comfortably;
one foot should be extended comfortably.
Having contracted that [leg], the second [leg] should be extended comfortably;
it is not permissible for a monk, at the head of the meal, or...
One should not stretch one's limbs while facing an image, or during the *sāmāyika* vow, or while listening to the Dharma.
Now, if a yawn comes upon a monk,
he may cover his mouth with the corner of his robe for comfort.
One should stretch. Now, if a monk experiences yawning again and again while seated at the head of the meal, [he should act as follows].
Having given one's bowl to the person sitting immediately next to oneself,
one may depart; or, having sat down for the purpose of hearing the Dharma,
one may depart after taking leave of those listening to the Dharma.
One must go; nor is it permissible for a monk, when entering an alms-round or entering among the houses, [to act otherwise].
Having entered,
while making the "maṭa-maṭā" sound and stretching one's limbs, one should yawn.
Now, if a monk experiences yawning again and again, he should cover his mouth with the corner of his robe and yawn with full awareness.
Now, if a monk who is sitting in a public place experiences yawning again and again,
he should rise and depart; he must not remain.
It is permissible for a monk to yawn before his preceptors, teachers, or those who are senior by stretching out his limbs with a "maṭa-maṭā" sound.
Now, if it is a monk...
When a yawn comes,
one should go to a secluded spot and yawn there; yet he does not act accordingly.
He transgresses the rules of proper conduct.
VII.10. Having accomplished the purpose for which he had come, the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One, dwells at Śrāvastī as the teacher of gods and humans.
He is honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated;
he has attained the highest gain and the highest fame, and is a recipient of them.
Regarding the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick,

he remains unsullied therein like a lotus by water; establishing beings who possess the fortune of merit in meritorious deeds, and settling beings who possess the fortune of the fruits in those very fruits.

Establishing beings who possess latent tendencies within those very tendencies, distributing the deathless nectar to many gods and humans, he causes hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of living beings to attain the deathless.

Having rescued them from the great abyss of the wilderness of saṃsāra— characterized by birth, old age, and death that have no beginning or end— and from the difficult-to-traverse hells, he establishes them in the secure, level, auspicious, and fearless ground of nirvāṇa, having thereby won them over.
In Aṅga, Magadha, Mallī, Varji, Kāśi, Kośala, Kuru, Pañcāla, Cedi, Vatsa, Matsya, Śūrasena, Śibi, Daśārṇa, Aśvaki, and Avanti, his prowess was witnessed;
he is the Self-Existent One (Svayaṃbhū).
He dwells in the divine abodes, the brahma abodes, the noble abodes, the imperturbable abodes, and the continuous abodes;
as a Buddha, he dwells in the abodes of a Buddha; as a Conqueror, he dwells in the abodes of a Conqueror; as a Knower, he dwells in the abodes of a Knower;
as the All-Knowing One, he dwells in the abodes of the All-Knowing One—having attained the supreme perfection of mastery over the mind.
Furthermore, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, dwell in whichever dwellings they desire;
yet those venerable ones of the group of six [do not].
With the intention of causing excitement,
they grind white flour, roasted barley meal, and boiled beans together and dry them in the sun;
when they have become dry, [they proceed].
Then they eat only white things; they eat *bilva* fruits; they eat fruits that have fallen naturally; or [they eat] *kalāpa* fruits.
They eat with sesame sprouts.
When the drum for the session has been struck,
they then go to the meditation hall and [look] toward the four directions.
They sit down. When the community of monks has taken their seats,
first one performs the act of foul-smelling wind, and another...
They go; another says, "They carry [it]"; another says, "Excellent!"
"Venerable one, what is this annual ritual? Even with eight hundred [instruments], one would not desire the wind;
oh, how pleasant is this sound! It makes things agreeable for those in the immediate vicinity."
They were making him smell a handful of lotuses.
He said, "Smell them, venerable sir! Oh, what a delicious fragrance! Oh!"
A pleasant fragrance disturbed the monks who were practitioners of yoga with its sound.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Summon the group of six."
“Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
“In that case, one should proceed with the ritual for wind in this manner. Now, what is it?”
In this way, one should proceed regarding the action concerning wind. It is not permissible for a monk to habitually consume white-colored groats or flour-meal.

Having dried the *mardīyā* fruits in the sun, it is not permissible to eat them while they are still white; nor is it permissible to eat *bilva* fruits, *madana* fruits, or any other fruits that are in their fresh, unripened state.
Or with peas, or with sesame sprouts.
Now, when a monk is wandering for alms and,
because his livelihood depends on others, receives white-colored boiled beans or crushed groats mixed with flour;
Even if one eats fruits that provoke wind (vāta),
there is no offense; however, it is not permissible for one seated in the practice of abandonment (prahāṇa) to do so with a mind of restlessness.
[If] a monk [wishes] to perform the work of a weaver for a ḍhara-ḍharāyī...
then now [it is permitted for] the monk.
If wind-disorder (vāta) arises while one is seated in the hall of exertion,
one must not now relax the sense-faculties (indriya).
Now, if one suffers from hemorrhoids,
being fully aware,
one should lift up one buttock, open it with the hand, and perform the evacuation of wind.
It must be done;
it must be done in such a way that the sound of the *ānantarya* [offense] does not carry out.
Now, it is not even permissible to lift up one's upper garment toward the side where an elder is seated. Rather,
indeed...
The one who is younger should lift up his buttocks toward the other.
Now, if the elder and the younger are both situated in the same place, [the following applies].

It is not permissible for a junior member of the Saṃgha to lift up his buttocks toward the senior of the Saṃgha; even if he lifts up his buttocks toward one who is older than himself [in general], it is still not permissible.
There is no offense. Now,
if a monk is unable to perform the emission of wind with full awareness,
he should go outside and perform the emission of wind.
Now, if a monk experiences flatulence again and again during the practice of exertion, he should inform [his fellow monks].
This is how one should go.
Furthermore, it is not permissible to perform the act of belching at the head of a meal or at the head of a drink with the intention of being frivolous.
In order to do so, one should indeed lift up even a single finger and perform the action of fanning.
Now, if the wind-action returns to the monk again, [it may affect] the bowl of the one sitting immediately next to him.
Having given [the gift], one should depart;
nor is it permissible [to stay] during the hearing of the Dharma.
While in the state of *sāmāyika*, whether out of a desire for levity or with a noisy sound (*phara-pharasya*),
one may perform the action of wind;
indeed, having lifted up one buttock, one performs the action of wind.
It must be performed.
Now, if a monk repeatedly experiences flatulence, [he should do so].

When [the teacher] arrives, one should depart after taking leave for the purpose of hearing the Dharma. It is not permissible to depart without having taken leave of one's preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya). Nor... [50a6]
It is not permissible for one sitting inside a house to perform the action of wind (flatulence) with a *phara-pharā* sound out of a desire for frivolity; rather, indeed,
[one should do so] by raising one buttock.
Having expelled [the wind], one should perform the action of passing wind with full awareness.
Now, if a monk must pass wind again and again, [he should do so].
He comes; having come to one side, he should perform [the action].
It is not permissible for the preceptor [to do so].
Or, in the presence of a teacher or an elder, with the intention of being frivolous, to make a blowing sound with the mouth;
now, if a monk...
If the wind begins to blow,
one should go to one side and perform it; it is no longer permissible to do it with the wind blowing upon oneself.
One should not be distracted by the fragrance; one should create a windbreak,
leaving a path for the wind.
Now, when a monk is traveling together with a caravan, this is the proper conduct: he must not [now...].
Standing at the head of the caravan, one should perform the work of fanning. Now,
if he suffers from hemorrhoids,
having opened [the anus] with his hand and having wiped it along the path, he should do so with full awareness.
Just as one would not disturb a caravan by means of its scent,
so too should one act after clearing the path of the wind.
In this way one should practice regarding the action of wind; yet one does not practice so.
He transgresses the rules of proper conduct.
The summary: (Thus) one should behave toward a lamp;
(thus one should behave toward a walking staff).
(II.p.76) Thus should one behave with respect to the bolster; thus should one behave with respect to the sitting mat; thus [should one behave] with respect to the preceptor...
This is how one should practice; this is how one should cough;
this is how one should sneeze.
In this way one should scratch;
in this way one should yawn;
in this way one should attend to the movement of wind.
The intermediate summary:
The Elder of the Saṃgha, bedding and seats, the kaṭhina robe, guests, forest-dwellers, residents, and the lamp— these seven groups have been elucidated.
The rules concerning proper conduct are completed.

Of those phenomena that arise from a cause,
the Tathāgata has declared their cause,
as well as their cessation.
The Great Śramaṇa speaks thus.
